I originally recorded this as Hypopachus variolosus (Sheep Frog).  
However, on reconsideration of the recording, I have come to think this may be Gastrophryne carolinensis instead. 

My original comments follows from when I thought it was Hypopachus -
"I have herped and birded this boardwalk many times.  I have recorded frogs here on more than one occasion.  I was very suprised to hear this species calling here.  This is a slightly brackish (?) coastal water treatment plant.  The most common snake species in this marsh is Nerodia clarkii.
I have no idea how this species came to be here?  While they do occur slight further north and east than this, I find it very odd for it to be on a barrier island.  Possibly it was transported in some plant material or soil?

There are also Hyla cinerea in this pond, however, so it isn't inhospitable to anurans.  Still a surprise.

The frog was only calling once ever 17 seconds, so I removed about 12 seconds of background noise/birds between calls.  It was not dark when I recorded this.

American Bullfrogs are secondary consumers, eating almost everything including insects, tadpoles, other frogs including the spring peeper, and even other bullfrogs. They are the largest of the north american frog species, and have a very distinct rumbling grunt for a call. They are typically greenish brown, and lack dorsal ridges, which distinguishes it from the green frog. The underside may have dark spots. The life cycle of a bullfrog begins with an egg, and then developing into a tadpole. After that stage, legs develop which transforms the tadpole into a froglet. After the froglet stage, the tail is lost, and it becomes a mature frog. The individual I heard was a mature adult frog. I was not able to sex it because I could not see the circles under the eyes. I assume that it was male because of the loud vocalization. The habitat of the American Bullfrog is aquatic, and they can be found in small ponds, creeks, rivers, streams, and other wet environment. They can also be found in marshlands and swamps. A predator of the bullfrog is the snapping turtle. A competitor of the bullfrog is the green frog.

A one minute sample of an 18 minute stereo recording. The general sound of the wetland marsh that night, mostly dominated by the banjo-like "twang" call of the Green Frogs. There is no adjustment of volume levels. There are an interesting variety of frog sounds, often quite close to the microphone, and in a beautiful stereo landscape of evening insects, with only the faint murmer of the nearby natural gas compressor station. 

The background meadow and wetland insects are as interesting as the frogs of course, as well as a number of geat incidental sounds such as frogs plopping about in the water right in front of the microphone. Very evocotive of the night time cattail marsh environment! 

Recorded with a RØDE Stereo Videomic Pro microphone mounted on a Canon EOS Rebel T3i camera shooting video. This microphone is able to overcome the noise of the camera's pre-amp to produce this superb quality digital audio. Try listening to this with headphones!

After drenching July rains, there were several different tree frog and toad sounds in these low damp woods near the Mattaponi River of Virginia. This evening's sky was then fairly clear. 

For this recording I placed my microphone within 1.5 meters of a 4 meter wide grassy ephemeral pool to record what sounded to me like a flock of sheep bleating! I knew they were not sheep, but could not spot anything at all in the pool with a torch. I later photographed something that looked sort of like a tiny-eyed Spring Peeper, but did not see it call. When I looked for similar sounds online, I quickly found out that these sheep were really Eastern Narrow-mouthed Toads! 

It sounds like there are 4 or 5 individuals in this recording, nicely spread out in stereophonic space, singing one after another, and overlapped, usually with 3-5 second pauses between groups of calls. There are also naturally some interesting insects in the background. This is a one minute sample of a twelve minute recording. 

I made a sonogram and discovered that each Toad is actually singing a chord composed of at least ten different notes at the same time (or harmonics? - I'm new to looking at sounds this way)!

By my count -- and I spent some time sorting through the 182 photographs of 129 records and combining images of the same (presumed) individuals -- I am submitting the following taxa from this spot (tentatively): 12 ants, 1 ant lion, 1 bee, 17 beetles, 7 "bugs," 1 cockroach, 1 dragonfly, 1 damselfly, 3 flies, 2 lacewings, 8 leafhoppers, 1 mantis, 70 (!) moths, 1 scorpion (on a fallen pine log 100 feet from the array; Clint found it with a UV light), 4 shield bugs, and 3 giant water bugs.

With Don Fraser, Clint Gibson, and many others; a nocturnal moth survey, organized by Virginia "Ginny" Hamilton of The Nature Conservancy. There were two moth arrays about 600 feet apart. I have ignored several tiny to small, generic-shaped beetles and other small insects, most of which probably could not be identified by my photographs. By my count -- and I spent some time sorting through all my photographs -- I am submitting 104 records (I combined images of the same [presumed] individuals in many cases): 62 moths, 1 ant, 1 ant lion, 10 beetles, 2 "bugs," 1 cockroach, 1 dragonfly, 4 flies, 2 frogs (audio), 2 leafhoppers, 1 mantidfly, 1 mayfly, 6 mosquitoes, 3 spiders (from the ground nearby), 1 "something," 1 treehopper, and 1 wasp.

All of these photographs were taken with my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 (with a broken exposure setting knob) and the built-in flash. The flash worked magically.

description:
I have been trying to make a decent recording of Bullfrogs in my neighborhood. I vividly remember hearing many of them when fishing and swimming in a farm pond near Taylorstown in the 1970s, and thought they would still be easy to hear in the summertime. Nowadays however, most of what I hear are Green Frogs. After many attempts, this is my first acceptable quality recording I have made of a (single lonely?) Bullfrog - in a cattail marsh in State Game Lands southeast of Washington, where it is generally quiet enough to make such recordings.  

This was at 8:28 P.M. Eastern Daylight Time (my camera is always set on Standard Time year 'round), which on that day was 16 minutes before actual local sunset at 8:44. Most of the frogs calling were Green frogs, but this one Bullfrog was booming about once every 45 seconds to a minute. I made a five minute recording, and simply spliced his calls together - six ten second excerpts from my recording to make a one minute composite sampler. One can still hear a few quiet Green Frog grunts and twangs, but it is edited such that the Bullfrog booms about every ten seconds or so. One can hear examples of the many birds that frequent the marsh as well, including the Red-winged Blackbird, Northern Cardinal, Rose-breasted Grosbeak, and Yellow Warbler. I don't like to post mixed bird choruses - this is meant as an observation of the Bullfrog only. 

I still hope to find a location where there are multiple Bullfrogs showing off their impressive sonorous vocal powers.
